chapter: Records and the claim that Black bands copied
title: Tiger Rag recording conditions, Kid Ory comparison and W.C. Handy's record
summary: He compares a recent Ory record with the 1918 Tiger Rag, describes acoustic recording setup, and plays a Handy Columbia record while disputing Handy's claims.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Making records: studios, takes and the technology

blocks.x: Playing a tiger rag. This is Dixonland Jubilee by Kit Ory. This is only about a year old. Between this and the one that I'll play that was played almost 42 years ago, 41 years ago, you'll see the difference. That's what these white men call good music. Some of these tribes should go back in Africa and live over there and find out about the Negro place over there. This man is coming Louis Armstrong. That's Armstrong. I'm sure the amount of people imitate from one night to the other. Here I'm talking about it. I shouldn't criticize any of the best I've been gone. It's only the friends of the public after 41 years. Negro has never invented anything new. Take Armstrong away from Africa. I'll now play you a record by the original Dixon Land jazz band, Tiger Rag, released in 1918, 1941. 40 years, almost 21 years. Listen to Angels, stop. This rhythm that I legal bands used for that, tuck, tuck, tuck, tuck, ta-da, ta-da. Now, when this record was made, it was made into an eight-inch horn. The most conditions that many musicians couldn't even play today. The cornet stood about 20 to 25 feet from the hound. The trombone was 15 feet. The clarinet had a separate little horn that coming out this eight-inch horn to about a four-inch bell. And he stood right near the piano. The piano faced me right under the hum. The drum stood alongside of me. And when the red light would have a white light burning, and when the red light came on, we were to all count two. And it's a miracle how we came in together. I'll never know. Maybe God was with us. I don't know. But you can see the difference. They have never improved on this plan. And I'll wager the last remaining years I got, game five men can play as good with all the electrical process, with all the improvements that they have in electrical recording, or any way they want to take it. These critics say we play rag time, but this is pristine jazz because all the roots are contained in two recordings. I'll play you the liver stable blues, which is the counterpart that takes up all the other licks that has ever been made up to this day, are in these two recordings. Go ahead. This is what I learned when I was in school. We used to sing a little song to the middle to the mclanic. Oh, what time is it? One of the boys used to have the idea. That was the first novelty record ever issued by any phonograph. Later came the laughing trombone, the crying saxophones, and whatnot. But this record led and pointed the way for other musicians to copy from. Okay, whenever you're ready. Talent Scotts was sent to New Orleans to find bands that could play our type of music. They recorded every white and every colored band. That can be attested by living people who have worked into phonograph places on Canal Street because there are several people who have expressed ideas on this thing. And they couldn't find no jazz bands in New Orleans. So they went to Memphis, Tennessee, and they selected W.C. Handy, who was to become the father of jazz and creator of the blues, and who couldn't either play blues or jazz. I'll let you hear his recording and then you judge for yourself.
